item.title: Why Old Wounds Can Hurt More Later in Life
item.description:
Aging

Why Old Wounds Can Hurt More Later in Life

Regrets and unresolved relationships can become more urgent as time shortens.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Gerontologist Malcolm Johnson developed the concept of “biographical pain” in later life.
  • Awareness of finitude can make regret and relational wounds feel newly urgent.
  • This distress may remain invisible unless it surfaces through mental or physical symptoms.
  • Trusted, non-judgmental listening can help a life story feel witnessed and accepted.

In my research with older people, I frequently encounter psychological phenomena that acquire a distinct intensity in later life.

‘My mother abandoned me throughout my life,’ Martha told me, wiping her eyes. ‘She always seemed to punish me by refusing to acknowledge me, refusing to see me. There is nothing more painful than feeling as though you are unseen by your mother.’

As our conversation unfolded, I felt the weight of the burden Martha carried, and a sense that she felt increasingly helpless in relation to what to do about it as the end of her life drew closer. She had unanswered questions, unresolved resentment, and a sense of panic and hopelessness about repairing wounds and making peace with the ghosts of her past.

Biographical Pain

The British gerontologist and later life scholar Professor Malcolm Johnson described such psychological and spiritual suffering as biographical pain. It is associated with the painful recollection of experienced wrongs, broken promises, regretted actions and unresolved relationships in the face of finitude.

In other words, it is the unique sense of suffering we experience towards the end of our lives, when we confront myriad loose ends, unanswered questions, unfulfilled ambitions, and the sense that our lives did not play out as we might have wished.

As Johnson suggested, not all lives are triumphs of attainment, love, and integrity. And in my research experience, many people are followed by a caravan of biographical pain by the time they reach the end of the journey.

What is unique about the phenomenon is that in later life we are forced to face the reality that we are nearing the end of the runway. There is little time to rewrite the script, change the course, or make amends.

In youth, the same issues are still very much a part of our biography, but there is a sense — a hypothetical possibility — that time will iron things out. It is as though we unconsciously believe we have time to make peace, resolve relational conflicts, and heal old wounds. And somehow, we can live with the loose ends, safe in the knowledge that we can deal with them if we need to.

But eventually, time runs out. And we are faced with the brutal reality that this is in fact our biographical story. Our script is written and we can no longer hide behind the defence of timelessness.

It is at this point in the lifespan that I have witnessed so many older people grappling with their own biographical pain. It might be related to unresolved relational wounds – like Martha’s – that are impossible to redress in person because, for example, the family and friends involved are long dead.

It could be our own guilt in relation to perceived wrongdoings, resentment in relation to harms we have experienced, or regret in relation to choices we wish we had made. There seems to be something about nearing the end of life that brings such issues to the surface powerfully. It is though we can no longer hide from them. Our soul seems to need to bring them to our attention.

Private Burden

I’ve noted that many older people carry this sort of burden silently and privately. Biographical pain is mostly invisible. Johnson argued that if it doesn’t manifest through physical and mental health symptoms, then it can go largely undetected and older people can suffer in silence. There is something particularly isolating about sitting alone and struggling with the unresolved burdens of one’s unique biographical journey.

Johnson believed that this sort of spiritual and psychological suffering does not simply go away on its own. In fact, for many people, the more it is revisited and the more time people sit with it alone and without a trustworthy witness, the more painful it gets.

One interviewee, Janet, told me: ‘All my life I've suffered…With everything that’s gone wrong, I would have liked to talk to somebody, no advice, I just feel I want to let off steam I suppose. But it doesn’t happen. There is no space you can talk privately. There's no space.’

Biographical Listening

In light of the fact that we cannot rewrite the script, one response that may help alleviate biographical pain is the simple practice of biographical listening. Ultimately, this amounts to non-judgmental listening with a trustworthy other who allows the teller the time and space to sort through, express, and explore their biographical pain.

In my experience, the result is often a sense that one’s biography has been shared, witnessed, unjudged, and accepted. This often brings a sense of comfort and relief around something that has often been carried privately for years. Although we cannot change the events already lived, biographical listening may alter how privately and painfully they must be carried.

If you would like to read more of Martha’s story, check out Reaching the End of the Runway at The Inner Room.

item.title: A Plague Scare Reminded Me to Get My Flu and COVID Vaccines
item.description:
Health

A Plague Scare Reminded Me to Get My Flu and COVID Vaccines

We fear rare infections while overlooking the common ones we can prevent.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Rare events, like a plague lab accident, create fear, while more common infections get less attention.
  • Flu and COVID cause hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations every year.
  • Flu and COVID vaccines are safe and reduce the risk of severe illness.
  • Flu and COVID vaccines lower the risk of heart attacks and other cardiac complications from these infections.

One of the biggest news stories in global health this past month was about a possible laboratory accident in Russia involving plague. Media outlets reported that a 28-year-old woman working at a plague research facility in Siberia died from pneumonic plague and that 200 people were placed under observation. Russian officials denied that the case was plague, attributing her death to "pneumonia of unknown origin."

Stories spread across mainstream media and social media about whether there might be a resurgence of the plague or the emergence of a new pathogen. How did I respond? I made an appointment at my local pharmacy to get the annual flu and COVID vaccines. Let me explain.

We Fear What’s Rare and Forget About What’s Common

A nurse administers the seasonal flu vaccine to a patient.
Source: CDC / Doug Jordan, M.A.

With many public policy problems, humans tend to react most viscerally to low-probability, high-consequence events. Think about the fear and intensity of media coverage that comes from airplane accidents compared with car accidents. Plane accidents are extremely uncommon. Most people do not fly very often and, even if they did, the National Safety Council estimates that the lifetime odds of dying in a plane crash are too small to even calculate.

Compare that with car accidents. Almost every American rides in a car regularly, and many spend several hours a day in one. The lifetime odds of dying in a motor vehicle crash are about 1 in 101. But a car accident barely registers in the news, and it usually only becomes something we discuss when we have a connection to the people or place involved.

In public health, we see a similar pattern. A bioweapon or dangerous pathogen accidentally spilling into the population and causing a pandemic is a real risk, but the likelihood of it happening is extremely small. (Note that the scientific consensus is that COVID emerged in nature and was not the result of an intentional or accidental laboratory incident.) If it does occur, it will generate enormous fear and attention, as happened with the incident in Russia.

The infectious diseases that most regularly make us severely ill or kill us, however, rarely get that intensity of reaction. Think about flu and COVID. Last winter, CDC estimates the flu season caused at least 32 million illnesses, 390,000 hospitalizations, and 24,000 deaths. For COVID, from mid-2024 to mid-2025, CDC estimated there were 290,000 to 450,000 hospitalizations and 34,000 to 53,000 deaths. While most people do not get hospitalized or die from these two respiratory viruses, many who get infected will still get sick, feeling miserable for days and missing school, work, or important social events. These illnesses have real costs to our lives.

What the Flu and COVID Vaccines Actually Do

We have vaccines for both of these infections that are safe and effective.

The flu vaccine has been given to hundreds of millions of people over decades, and its safety record reflects that. Most people experience a sore arm, mild fatigue, or a low-grade fever for a day or two. It is not biologically possible for the vaccine to cause the flu. When people report getting the flu soon after the vaccine, it is most often because flu is circulating in the community around the same time they are getting the vaccine.

How well the flu vaccine works varies from year to year, depending on how closely the vaccine matches the strains that end up circulating. Last season was a poor match because most circulating influenza A viruses belonged to a new strain that differed from the vaccine strain. Even so, among adults, the vaccine reduced the risk of flu-associated hospitalization by 30 percent. Even a small benefit can help you individually and the community overall.

The COVID vaccines have been studied almost as much as any vaccine in history. The side effects are similar to the flu vaccine. While there is a rare risk of myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle), the risk of getting myocarditis from the virus itself, not the vaccine, is far greater. As for effectiveness, a large CDC study of the 2024–25 COVID vaccine found effectiveness of 33 percent against emergency department and urgent care visits and, in elderly adults, 45 percent against hospitalization.

Other Benefits of the Flu and COVID Vaccines

Respiratory viruses trigger inflammation in the body that can destabilize the heart and blood vessels, which is why many studies have found that heart attacks rise in the weeks after a flu or COVID infection. Vaccination can protect against that risk.

A meta-analysis of randomized trials found that flu vaccination was associated with a 26 percent lower risk of heart attack and a 33 percent lower risk of cardiovascular death. For COVID, a study of nearly 2 million infected patients found that full vaccination reduced the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events by 41 percent.

Effective Does Not Mean Perfect

Let me be blunt. Effective does not mean 100 percent effective. Almost nothing in medicine works every time, for every person. Statins do not prevent every heart attack, and seat belts do not prevent every death in a car crash. We use them and we use vaccines because they shift the odds in favor of health and safety.

You can still get the flu or COVID if you are vaccinated. But you are less likely to end up in the hospital, less likely to die, and less likely to have heart-related complications.

When you hear about a potentially deadly infectious disease emerging, it is important to pay attention. The risks are real, and we need to invest more in the systems to prepare for, detect, and respond to them. In our daily lives, though, there is very little any of us can do to mitigate that risk.

There are steps we can take to reduce the complications of the infectious diseases we face every winter and keep ourselves healthier. That is why the news about plague prompted me to get my annual flu and COVID vaccines. I urge you to do the same.

item.title: Why 'You Can See Everything' Is So Psychologically Unsettling
item.description:
Forensic Psychology

Why 'You Can See Everything' Is So Psychologically Unsettling

A new documentary presents Elizabeth Holmes as shape-shifter extraordinaire.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • The psychological discomfort of watching "You Can See Everything" is real and raw.
  • The film forces viewers to witness psychological shape-shifting used as a survival mechanism.
  • Viewers may be left wondering whether there's a real self behind Holmes's many masks.
Psyche's Awakening
Source: Harper Collins

In the recently released documentary You Can See Everything, as we watch Elizabeth Holmes navigate her final days of freedom, our brains are starved of the evolutionary indicators we naturally rely on to detect truth, safety, and authenticity.

From a forensic evaluation standpoint, we look for four critical pillars to assess the risk of reoffending: true acknowledgment (clearly stating "I did it" rather than scapegoating others), empathy for those harmed, an admitted need for personal change, and prolonged, aligned action to support that change. These pillars reveal whether genuine transformation is occurring; a phrase like "mistakes were made" is simply not an adequate measure of true human change.

The documentary feels more like an eerie psychological thriller. From a behavioral standpoint, the film is deeply unsettling: Communication feels calculated, yet entirely serene. In psychology, behavioral mimicry—or the "chameleon effect"—is an unconscious habit used to fit into social environments. However, when this is taken to a pathological extreme, it becomes masking. Holmes operates as a master of this defense mechanism. She doesn't just lie; she alters her entire identity framework depending on who is watching. The unsettling feeling the audience experiences is the realization that her persona is a highly effective psychological shield. It is driven not by authentic selfhood, but by a deep-seated fear of rejection and an underdeveloped, unstable identity.

Elizabeth Holmes, a Modern-Day Mestra

To truly understand Holmes’s behavior in this documentary, we can look to the Greek myth of Mestra. Mestra was a shape-shifter, gifted by Poseidon, the god of the sea, with the ability to transform into any animal, figure, or form at will. She uses this power tactically: Her starving father sells her into slavery; she endures assault, abuse, and a loss of her sovereignty. However, with powers gifted to her by Poseidon, she transforms into a fisherman to escape, returns home, and repeats the cycle to survive. Take the Quiz + Find out Which Greek Myth Archetype Are You?).

Author Gillian O'Shea Brown
Source: Gillian O' Shea Brown, photographed by Zeeshaan Shabbir

To the outside world, shape-shifting looks like the ultimate superpower. However, when brought into the realm of psychology, "shape-shifting" is a defense mechanism and a survival strategy, not a superpower. Far from being a magical gift, psychological shape-shifting usually comes at a steep emotional cost. For many people, changing who they are isn't a choice made from a place of power—it is a mandatory response to a world that feels unsafe. Holmes acts as a literal manifestation of this archetype. When the "Tech Titan" form failed her, she shape-shifted into the "Betrayed Idealist," and finally into the "Soft, Sunny Mother" we see on the beach.

For Holmes, as for Mestra, transforming her identity is an act of extreme, albeit maladaptive, survival. She treats Nathan Fielder’s camera as just another master to outsmart, using a new shape to buy the public's empathy and escape her narrative cage. But underneath the shape-shifter lies a poor sense of self. This psychological masking is driven by Holmes's deep fear of rejection and poor sense of self. A poor sense of self in psychology often stems from unresolved childhood trauma and usually means a person has an underdeveloped, unstable identity. They will lack a clear understanding of their own preferences, values, strengths, and boundaries outside of others. Over time, they become a "shape-shifter" with a rapidly shifting, poorly developed sense of self.

The ultimate reason we cannot look away—and why we feel so deeply disturbed—is that the documentary exposes a profound psychological hollow. We aren't just unsettled because we can't tell who is lying; we are unsettled because the concept of "truth" has been completely erased by the subject. In mythology, Mestra always retained her true human core when she shifted back. But a real-world psychological shape-shifter often looks in the mirror and feels entirely "blank."

Because Holmes has spent a lifetime changing shapes to manipulate her environment, she appears to exhibit identity diffusion, a painful state in which an individual genuinely does not know who they are when the audience leaves the room. When viewers watch those agonizing, unblinking staring contests between Holmes and Fielder, the discomfort comes from the creepy realization that there is no "real" Elizabeth Holmes underneath the camouflage to find.

item.title: Does Your Therapist Support Abuse?
item.description:
Domestic Violence

Does Your Therapist Support Abuse?

A therapist’s response to abuse may mean you need someone else.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Abuse is not normal; it's a choice.
  • Before a person can have a good relationship, they must have a safe relationship.
  • Some therapists do not understand the harm of abuse because they are part of the society that normalizes it.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Years ago, while walking my dog in the park, I saw a man slap a woman so hard across the face that she stumbled backwards.

My dog and I stopped still in our tracks, and we stared at both of them until the most uncomfortable person (the man) turned away. I continued to stare, and as they drove away, I picked up a stick and scratched out his license plate number in the dirt on the side of the road.

Justice Is Served

As luck would have it, just then a park ranger drove by on his quad. I flagged him down and asked him to call the police. (This was before cell phones.) Minutes later, a squad car showed up, and the man was immediately put in custody and charged with domestic violence. He pled “not guilty” until I showed up in court.

A few days later, the victim called my office to pass along a “thank you” message. She sheepishly added that she, too, was a psychologist.

Abuse in America

There are over 1 million mental health professionals in the United States. They’re a diverse lot, but they all have one thing in common: They all come out of the general population, which is experiencing a pandemic in behavioral health pathology in the form of intimate partner violence.

According to The National Domestic Violence Hotline, about 24 individuals are victimized by an intimate partner every minute in the U.S. This adds up to over 12 million people each year. However, this statistic does not tally up the many incidents of emotional or verbal abuse, where there is no violence, so one can assume that abuse occurs even more frequently than reported.

Sharing What I've Learned

After 35 years as a marriage and family therapist, I began sharing my thoughts on having healthy relationships on social media. I naively thought, at the time, that we were all in agreement that abuse was a terrible scourge in our country. Turns out, this wasn't the case.

I was surprised to read the comments where people argued that yelling and screaming, specifically, were vital to “sharing who we really are and getting real with our feelings.” I was even more surprised at the many comments from individuals who commented that, in couples counseling, their therapist sometimes saw and heard abuse in the session and said nothing about it—sometimes going so far as to blame the victim for the verbal abuse. One therapist even scoffed, “An abuse-free life? That’s not a thing.”

Abuse Is Not Normal

So, here I am, reminding everyone that any and all abuse is not normal; it is maladaptive and shuts off the prefrontal cortex—the "smart" part of the brain—in favor of the amygdala, also known as the "lizard brain" that is driven by fight or flight.

Abuse, including verbal abuse, like yelling and screaming, triggers this switch. When this happens, the couple’s ability to engage in problem-solving (also known as conflict resolution) is heavily compromised, if not disabled. When it happens in the therapist’s office and nothing is said, the abuse becomes normalized and part of a pattern known as gaslighting.

No Relationship Benefits From Abuse

I have learned throughout my career that abuse doesn’t start with a punch to the face. Odds are, the woman whom I saw get slapped in the park was unaware of the dangers of abuse, and how yelling, screaming, and put-downs can eventually lead to a slap to the face.

But Steve, wasn’t she a therapist? How could she not know? Because she, like every other therapist, is from the general population where abuse is normalized.

Before we can have a good relationship, we must have a safe relationship, and we cannot have safe relationships when there is abuse. We cannot resolve the conflicts that keep us apart when there is abuse. Abuse is perhaps the single most self-defeating pattern of behavior in relationships.

Ask Your Therapist

If you’re in therapy or seeking therapy, I urge you to ask your therapist where they stand on abuse. You may need another therapist if any of the following are true:

  • Your therapist isn’t confronting abusive behavior in your session
  • Your therapist isn’t screening your relationship for abuse prior to couples counseling
  • Your therapist does anything to minimize the significance of abuse

Therapists who do not understand the harm of abuse are woefully lacking in the necessary training, skills, and courage you need from your therapist. Remember, abuse is not normal. In fact, it’s a choice. I urge you to make the right one in this matter.

The National Domestic Violence Hotline is ready to receive calls (in English or Spanish) 24 hours every single day. Call 1-800-799-7233. To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: 3 Practical Solutions to Fix Marriage Boredom
item.description:
Boredom

3 Practical Solutions to Fix Marriage Boredom

Relationships transform when you start viewing boredom as an opportunity.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Greater emotional closeness can coexist with reduced intimacy when routines crowd out novelty.
  • Growth apart and together can rekindle attraction by helping partners see each other anew.
  • Avoiding conflict to preserve intimacy can worsen relationship problems rather than protect closeness.
Source: Tima Miroshnichenko / Pexels

Many couples come to therapy worried about having gotten “too close for comfort.” They might express their concern by saying things like:

  • “I’m just not as excited to come home from work anymore. We love each other, but we live the exact same day over and over again.”
  • “We used to have so much fun together, but we’re both so tired now that we just stay at home.”
  • “Our sex life has really changed over the years; I can’t remember the last time we really enjoyed ourselves.”

These statements are reminiscent of the “intimacy paradox,” whereby increased closeness in a relationship coexists with a lack of intimacy. As couples become more emotionally connected, they often settle into repetitive routines, inadvertently creating boredom or reduced intimacy.

It is important to acknowledge these lulls in a relationship. Marital boredom has been linked to lower levels of relationship satisfaction, and a 2023 study found that it can lead to an increase in frustration, negative exchanges, diminished mood, and impaired judgment. It may also have repercussions for individual and relational well-being by eroding intimacy and commitment and raising the likelihood of infidelity and divorce.

To successfully navigate the “intimacy paradox” of marital boredom, consider these three questions.

1. Are You Playing It Too Safe?

A 2010 study found that relationship boredom is usually a function of not meeting one’s psychological need for novelty and variety.

A 2020 study also highlighted that lower levels of “self-expansion” in a relationship were linked to lower relationship satisfaction. Self-expansion refers to the inclination to seek out new experiences, relationships, and opportunities for personal growth that help individuals expand and enrich their sense of self. Romantic relationships allow for self-expansion as individuals can learn from, adapt to, and be influenced by their partners.

However, if one is stuck in a monotonous routine with their partner, they are likely neither growing individually nor together. In new relationships, partners have greater opportunities to learn from each other, but in long-term relationships, as self-concepts become increasingly intertwined, seeking individual growth is crucial.

Contrary to popular belief, research shows that boredom can be positive, serving as a motivator for change and positive risk-taking in relationships. Engaging in new activities, both separately and together, can help rekindle the spark by creating opportunities for self-expansion. Being dynamic allows partners to see each other in a new light, sharing new experiences and perspectives that cut through boredom.

A 2021 study highlights how sometimes, to cope with relationship boredom, partners respond with more inaction or choose shared experiences that are safe, comfortable, and familiar, which have previously guaranteed excitement or intimacy for both partners. While relationship safety is essential, researchers suggest that when one experiences less growth or self-expansion than expected, boredom sets in.

Growth expectations can evolve over time, and developing a habit to check in with your partner about their goals, interests, and dreams can keep the relationship exciting.

2. Are You Avoiding The Problem?

The intimacy paradox persists when partners try to sweep it under the rug instead of addressing what might be causing the slump proactively through communication.

Research shows that solely trying to preserve intimacy while entirely avoiding conflict only creates more relationship problems and leads to coping poorly with stress as a couple. This affects individual and relationship well-being and is often a result of fearing rejection or abandonment by a partner. However, it is necessary to tolerate the discomfort of addressing both your feelings, as it allows you to have your needs met and brings you closer to a resolution.

Further, individuals may also be avoiding dissatisfaction stemming from other areas of their lives, with feelings of boredom or stagnancy spilling over into the relationship instead. There could also be areas of a partner's life that are avoided or going unnoticed in conversation, creating communication blocks and repetitive conversations. Cultivating more curiosity about a partner, no matter how long you have known them, can deepen romantic connection.

3. Are You Taking Your Partner For Granted?

The value of a relationship is sometimes overshadowed by its monotony. Making a conscious choice to prioritize one’s partner daily and shifting one’s mindset from “I have to work on my relationship” to “I get to be with my partner” is a fundamental step in reigniting a sense of excitement and appreciation for the privilege of being together.

Further, being responsive to a partner's needs, emotions, and desires fosters a resilient emotional connection where both partners feel heard and valued, combating feelings of boredom and disconnection.

Engaging in capitalization—or the act of sharing positive events, accomplishments, and good news with a partner—also amplifies your relationship experience. Celebrating each other's successes can create a sense of mutual appreciation.

Lastly, plan positive events like vacations or date nights to show appreciation. While planning might seem to counter the spontaneity of exciting activities, it actually creates a more conducive environment where couples can organically explore and have unhurried moments of enjoyment. Conscious planning allows them to engage in the self-expanding experiences that bring them back to each other.

Addressing boredom in your marriage requires self-reflection, a willingness to embrace novelty, and mutual proactive efforts to strengthen one’s connection. If treated as an opportunity for growth, boredom acts as a catalyst for deeper intimacy, where both partners feel cherished and energized, helping to dispel the monotony that creeps into long-term relationships and instead creating a renewed sense of joy.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: Would You Read Your Partner’s ChatGPT?
item.description:
Relationships

Would You Read Your Partner’s ChatGPT?

Private AI conversations can leave both partners feeling betrayed.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Discussion about an intimate relationship with a chatbot is a new type of betrayal.
  • In a partnership, both people can experience pain and a sense of infidelity when chatbots provide advice.
  • Betrayal involving AI conversations is less likely to have been discussed in a relationship before it happens.
Source: Unsplash/Arhihou Anas

In Lindsey Hall’s viral Substack post, “I Stumbled Across My Boyfriend's ChatGPT, and It Ended Our Relationship,” the author describes what it was like to accidentally come across numerous saved chat logs in which her partner was seeking support and advice from ChatGPT about their relationship. Chat gets very involved, and after Hall’s partner shares some doubts, Chat guided, "Then you should consider ending it."

In my sex and relationship therapy practice, I am seeing a new type of betrayal. As more people use chatbots for therapy and guidance (the number one use case for the past two years), it becomes easier to access our partners’ private thoughts. What would otherwise be a totally confidential conversation with another person instead becomes an ongoing written dialogue, often happening while we are in the room, without our awareness.

Practical barriers to our partners’ thoughts and feelings have been removed. Instead of actively seeking out our partner’s diary and deciding whether to read it, or eavesdropping on a conversation with a friend, we go into ChatGPT and find our partner’s last thread.

Would You Turn Away?

One of the most challenging aspects of intimacy and relationships is accepting that parts of our partners’ inner lives will always remain unknowable. Despite the reassurance and control we desire or come to rely on, we can never have complete certainty about the future of our relationship.

There is something deeply appealing about knowing. If there is even a hint of doubt in a relationship, it can be compelling to seek additional information in an attempt to find that assurance.

All of this is to say that it’s hard to turn away when presented with an open chat, especially when we recognize familiar names in the conversation and uncertainty is front and center. Our personal attachment styles and relationship dynamics can make it even harder to close the chat without reading.

The Ghost in the Machine

In her book Artificial Intimacy, researcher Sherry Turkle posits that “chatbots provide mirrors rather than relationships.” It has become a well-established theory that chatbots offer a reflection of us. Shaped by user prompts to behave in a certain way and fed the types of questions we want answered, chatbots work hard to give us what we want.

“The fact this was on ChatGPT, in its own way, made the whole thing feel even more grotesque and surreal. It was like accidentally reading someone’s diary, except the diary was a [expletive] robot—predisposed to agree with him, ready to take his cruel thoughts and shape them into something that sounded reasonable.” — Lindsey Hall

If what we are reading is a mirror of our partner’s thoughts, it follows that a log of these conversations might offer one of the most intimate looks into our partner’s psyche that we can get. Or is it just a misleading spiral perpetuated by chatbots’ sycophantic tendency to keep users engaged, refusing to end the conversation? It is natural for the partner discovering the chat logs to experience anger or even a feeling of betrayal towards the chatbot itself.

Betrayal

In any case, most people do not seek advice from their chatbot with the expectation that others will read it. For many, the feeling that has led them to this conversation is one of questioning or even angst. They are trying to figure out their feelings and want a space in which to do so, with few or no parameters.

There are two types of perceived human betrayal in these instances:

  1. Discovering that your partner has shared intimate details of your relationship with their chatbot
  2. Realizing that your partner has read your private chat logs

In a partnership, both people can experience pain and a sense of betrayal: one from having their private life shared with a chatbot without their consent, and the other from having their private thoughts exposed and witnessed.

Source: Unsplash/Shamblen Studios

This type of betrayal is less likely to have been discussed in a relationship before it happens. As more and more people share their thoughts about personal relationships with chatbots, conversations about these boundaries within relationships become increasingly necessary.

So, What Do We Do?

Talk to your partner about their relationship with their chatbot. Ask yourself: Are there topics you wouldn’t want your partner to discuss with their chatbot? If the answer is yes, discuss them with your partner. Ask your partner if they have questions for you about your own relationship with a chatbot.

An open dialogue can bring us together. Otherwise, as conversations become more siloed with our machine confidants, we can easily find ourselves moving further and further apart.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Fatigue Spectrum in Chronic Stress and Trauma
item.description:
Stress

The Fatigue Spectrum in Chronic Stress and Trauma

Learn how pacing expands your capacity for ongoing sustainability.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic stress, PTSD, and burnout can all manifest as fatigue from mild to the point of a medical diagnosis.
  • Exertion-related crashes can be delayed, so pacing requires tracking patterns beyond today's energy.
  • Pacing covers emotional, cognitive, physical, social, and spiritual effort, not only physical activity.

Chronic stress, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and burnout don't just stay in the head. At some point, the overloaded body systems stop working, and that manifests as fatigue. Eventually, you end up in a state of chronic fatigue.

At the low end of the scale, it's easy to ignore; you wake up tired after a full night's sleep. A bit further down the scale is burnout, or what Sweden calls exhaustion disorder (Eskilsson et al., 2017). Then, at the far end of the scale, you have a medical diagnosis of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS).

Stress and the Body

People with PTSD have significantly raised levels of inflammatory mediators (Passos et al., 2015), and inflammation in itself is linked to fatigue (Cho et al., 2013). Both childhood trauma and PTSD are associated with a greatly increased risk of CFS (Dansie et al., 2012; Heim et al., 2009). ME/CFS is a biological illness rather than a psychological one (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, n.d.). The systems aren't separate, of course, and a body that's been under chronic stress for years may have very few reserves left to recover.

People with ME/CFS and long COVID will refer to what happens when you do too much as a "crash." The medical term is post-exertional malaise (PEM), and it can occur days later. In one survey of people with ME/CFS, 90 percent reported experiencing PEM following both mental and emotional exertion (Chu et al., 2018). Burnout isn't ME/CFS in another guise, but anyone who's been running on depleted reserves for years will have felt that delayed bill. That's the approach I'm taking, not the diagnosis.

Three tiers of sustainability
Source: Dr. Odelya Gertel Kraybill

Three Tiers of Sustainability

An Individualized Sustainability Plan (ISP) in the ETI approach is built on three levels of activity:

  1. Enjoyment is the "right now" stuff—what just feels good.
  2. Self-care is also enjoyable and provides consistency (sleep, food, movement, people, time in nature).
  3. Sustainability is the level of contemplation; it's about observing what works, what doesn't, and why.

The tiers aren't a hierarchy; all of them are absolutely essential. The issue is that people keep lumping them together, and that confusion often causes pacing to fall apart. Pacing is present in all of the tiers, as we don't just use our energy in one way.

Pacing the Whole Person

Chronic stress will always take away enjoyment first, viewing it as the "optional" one. It isn't. A nervous system that has never known pleasure doesn't know what safety is. What was once restorative can quietly become depleting—like a long phone call with a loved one, where you absorb their pain alongside your own. Emotional pacing in this scenario doesn't mean less joy; it means your joy comes in measured doses the system can cope with.

Self-care is where the push-and-crash cycle does the most damage. You decide to walk every day, cook properly, and get to bed at a reasonable time. Then you have a bad week, and the whole thing comes crashing down because you've built it for your best days. Physical pacing is very much in the long COVID camp. You work out what you can do on a fairly normal, slightly tough day, then build up slowly from there without fixed increases. A five-minute-a-day routine can survive a crash week. An hour-a-day routine often cannot.

Cognitive load is also part of self-care. Chronic stress constricts your attention and depletes your working memory, so every decision costs you. Writing things down so your memory doesn't have to carry them is self-care. So is making a decision once, rather than every morning, and reserving your clearest hours for the most demanding thinking.

Social pacing is easy to ignore. NICE gives it a name for a reason (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2021). Being around people drains energy, even if you want to be there. The parents of a child with a chronic illness spend hours explaining the illness to people who are genuinely well-meaning and who still end up asking the completely wrong questions. Pacing in this context might mean leaving the party while you still have enough energy to get home, without having to explain yourself to anyone.

And then there's spiritual pacing. By spiritual, I mean whatever gives your life meaning. There's a massive pressure to find the meaning in what's happened, to grow from it and make it into something. That pressure in itself is a massive drain on your energy. Spiritual pacing focuses on mapping what feels right and feels wrong by observing what it is, noticing how it feels, and responding accordingly.

Where Pacing Supports Sustainability

Sustainability is the tier people don't focus on. It doesn't feel good in the moment, and it also contains the other two. Because of the delay, we can't really pace ourselves based on how we feel at any one point in time. It's all down to observation over time.

For trauma survivors, this very act of noticing can be in itself an act of repair. We were taught very early on to override the body's signals because they weren't safe or useful to attend to. Learning to read them again, without judgment, is a very slow process.

Reflection also changes what you do on a good day. A good day is information, not a license to go out and sort through every single debt in one go. You spend some of the extra, you keep some in the bank. A crash is not evidence of failure. It just tells you where the edge is. The shame that follows is just another withdrawal from an account which was already very low.

Reflection is the bridge to contemplation; while reflection involves actively listening to your thoughts and experiences, contemplation is a state of deep inner looking in which you understand and absorb what you have reflected on.

Contemplation

In chronic burnout, we're in a state of pain of some kind. It can be hidden, and we can be numb, or completely overwhelmed. Contemplation is not about finding a way out of that state. It's about noticing how we're feeling right now without judgment. Judgment takes us straight out of the present moment and into withdrawal. There's nothing wrong with that. We're absolutely allowed to withdraw, to regress, to shut down. The point is to increase our capacity to notice without judgment, even without judging the judgment. The more we can do that, the more we can contemplate. The more we can contemplate, the more we can expand sustainability.

item.title: The Six Things We Forget About Ourselves
item.description:
Intuition

The Six Things We Forget About Ourselves

Personal Perspective: Remembering these truths moves you toward self-trust.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Complex decisions involve more information than conscious reasoning can hold at once.
  • Turning inward for answers often brings up rumination and self-doubt instead of clarity.
  • Research on optimal self-esteem points to beliefs that make it safer to trust oneself.

A few years ago, I found myself in a place where I had to make a really tough decision.

We had just bought the home of our dreams and were going to move in a couple of weeks. Then circumstances changed. My husband and I began wondering whether moving in was the right thing to do.

I wish the answer had been a clear yes or an outright no. It would have spared me sleepless nights and endless arguments with myself, and sometimes with my husband.

Eight days went by. All the thinking, analyzing, and weighing the pros and cons had completely exhausted me. I wished someone would wave a magic wand and the perfect answer would fall from the skies.

The next day, it did. I was standing at my window, looking out as dusk descended on the evening in a warm embrace of soft peachy pink. And I broke down in tears.

Partly exhaustion. Largely relief.

Some people call this intuition. I like to call it the soul’s knowing. Because something in us always knows. We just don’t have faith in it—unless all our other ways have left us nowhere.

When I felt calmer, I looked back out the window, and suddenly but softly, my soul spoke.

Moving in is not the right thing at this time.

Instead of the perfect answer that I was desperate for, I had found an answer that just felt right. And that was enough.

And in that moment, I realized that right has a conviction to it that perfect can never match.

Most of us face, will face, or have faced decisions that are ambiguous and complicated. Decisions that involve other people. Decisions that contain conflicting needs, values, or longings.

Trying to work through them with our reasoning capacities will almost always bring us to our knees because reason was never made for complexity. It was made for simpler problem-solving. Which flight will get me into Seattle in time for my meeting?

But most of the important decisions we face are far more complex. The data is so vast that the conscious brain cannot hold it all in one place.

This is why we can keep revisiting our decisions, especially in the silence of the night when the less tangible and measurable aspects of the situation rise in importance.

The head doesn’t know what to do with them, so it ignores them, even though these are the very aspects that can point us in the right direction because they are connected to the deepest longings of our heart.

Most of us will struggle to access our intuition because it surfaces in the quieter, self-referential part of the brain known as the default mode network. But the network that offers insight and houses our sense of self is also where rumination lives. So instead of hearing our inner voice, we hear self-criticism and self-doubt.

We can grow up in perfectly secure homes with love and laughter. And we can still be stuck trying to engineer control into a decision that needs something entirely different.

The trust that, regardless of what happens, we will be okay.

Intuition needs a different set of beliefs because fear and intuition exist on two different continuums. One helps us function. The other helps us flourish.

Based on my research on Optimal Self-Esteem, I have identified the six implicit beliefs that are in service of self-actualization. I call them soul truths because we are born with them.

6 Soul Truths

Here are the six soul truths. I invite you to see which one(s) you have forgotten and/or will help you most at this time in your life.

1. All Is Well

There is no courtroom. Nothing here is on trial, and that includes me.

People with this belief can be in a situation before deciding whether it is good or bad. They hear criticism without it becoming a verdict and praise without needing it as proof.

2. I Am Good

My inherent nature is beautiful. I do not have to prove it.

This is someone who does not feel the need to be or look a certain way, or achieve certain things, to win love or feel they belong. Someone who can admit a mistake without it meaning anything about their sense of self-worth.

3. I Am Love

I give love, and I receive love. It is what I am made of.

This is the person for whom love is the full expression of who they are. They can give love without demands attached, receive love without feeling undeserving of it, and set boundaries where boundaries are needed.

4. I Matter

I have a place in the world. My presence makes a difference.

People who know they matter have a certain drive and fierceness that no amount of external rewards can impart. They are shining their own light in their way for their own tribe.

5. I Can

Challenges and setbacks do not make me smaller. I grow through it all.

This is someone who meets life with a sense of agency rather than helplessness. They have an abiding trust in their ability to grow through it all.

6. I Trust

Life will meet me, and I can meet it. I am held as I hold.

This is the person who is fully open to whatever life brings their way. They are not waiting for the right conditions. They are not hooked on a certain outcome. They are the embodiment of a flourishing person, taking themselves lightly and their work seriously.

None of these soul truths need to be learned. They simply need to be remembered, because the stronger your ground, the higher your growth.

A Prompt to Explore

Think of a situation where you feel stuck or slowed down. What is the soul truth you have forgotten? What does grounding yourself in it open up for you? What is the insight that emerges?

item.title: Predator, Prey, and the Fear System in the Wild
item.description:
Fear

Predator, Prey, and the Fear System in the Wild

Natural mechanisms that reset our fear responses after major threats.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • The fear system can reset following fear collapse in two different ways.
  • We can recover through a powerful fear-arousal response.
  • We can recover in a safe place through deep breathing and tremoring.
  • Both are relevant to our work in therapy.
Source: YouTube 100100 Channel - LogoDalil Agency

I want to share two nature videos that vividly demonstrate the fear system in action. They illustrate the fear responses humans share with other animals, particularly the biological mechanisms that reset the fear system after a major threat.

I am using the term ‘fear system’ to cover three responses to danger or threat. The first (not illustrated in the videos) is fear alert, which is our response to danger sensed at a distance. We go very still, hold our breath, and try to locate the threat; meanwhile, our startle response is readied.

The second, once the danger is clearly perceived, is fear arousal; the sympathetic nervous system triggers a powerful, sudden physical mobilisation to escape the danger. The third response, when the danger is too close to escape, is fear collapse; the parasympathetic nervous system triggers this shutdown. It also switches a predator’s attack and opens the possibility of a last-ditch escape—and a less fearful, painful death.

Switching from Fear Collapse to Fight-or-Flight

In the first example (click here, but I recommend turning off the sound [1]), we see an antelope in fear arousal (fight-or-flight), being chased by a cheetah, then in fear collapse, caught with its throat in the cheetah’s jaws. The cheetah, exhausted by the pursuit, is then chased off by a hyena. The hyena is about to rip into the antelope’s stomach but is distracted by the cheetah and chases it off again. However, this ‘window of opportunity’ prompts a sudden shift in the antelope from fear collapse to fear arousal, and it makes off at high speed. With both cheetah and hyena nearby, this is not a safe place, but the escape burns off the energy of the fight-or-flight response, and once in a safe place, the antelope’s fear system will reset, ready for the next threat, without any ongoing trauma.

Recovering from Fear Collapse in a place of safety

In the second example (click here), a leopard has already caught an antelope, which is in fear-collapse and lying as if lifeless, eyes open, with its nose in the leopard’s jaws. A hyena is spotted, and the leopard is distracted – notice how, when the leopard releases its grip to look at the hyena, the antelope’s head flops onto the ground. In the metabolic shutdown of fear collapse, the muscles lose their 'tone' or tension – hence the flop.

The leopard is then further distracted by a couple of baboons, which chase it off. The antelope is left lying in the fear-collapsed state, completely still at first. After a few moments, its abdomen moves, it starts breathing deeply, and you see eyelids flicker. Eventually, as it starts to right itself, it shudders for almost a full minute, moving into gentle tremoring; this is the fear system ‘resetting’. Finally, the antelope is up and away.

The Fear-System Reset in Psychotherapy

It is helpful to understand these two natural mechanisms which reset the fear system, as the deactivation of fear responses which have become ‘stuck’ after traumatic experiences is a key task of psychotherapy.

The first video shows a window of opportunity for escape opening in an unsafe setting, with a sudden switch from fear collapse and back into fight-or-flight. Therapists use this pathway out of collapse, switching back into fight-or-flight, to help clients connect with and express anger or aggressive impulses in a safe context (here is an example in my post on retaliatory responses).

The second video shows a recovery from fear collapse in what is now a safe place (protected by baboons). The recovery starts with deep spontaneous breaths that expand the abdomen, followed by a period of shaking or trembling in which the tension and energy of the fight-or-flight impulse dissipate, and the fear system is ‘reset’.

In humans, we see the trembling or tremoring response in the immediate aftermath of a traumatic event, for example, a car accident, when a victim receives good roadside care and starts to feel safe again. Psychologist and medical biophysicist Peter Levine warns against misinterpreting trembling and treating it with medical intervention, which can interrupt the recovery [2].

Certain practices aim to replicate this natural trauma-recovery mechanism and are widely used to help emergency first responders process secondary trauma from their work [3, 4].

Less commonly, we observe tremoring in the therapy room, though it can manifest subtly, such as gentle trembling or a flush of heat that may not be noticed or understood [5]. In my own practice, I was made aware of it by clients who reported trembling when safe in bed at night after experiencing a breakthrough in their therapy session.

item.title: If You're Around 50, Here's Why Happiness Dips
item.description:
Midlife

If You're Around 50, Here's Why Happiness Dips

Midlife can feel heavy, and you’re far from alone. Research suggests it lifts.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Research across 145 countries finds well-being generally follows a U-shaped curve over a human adult life.
  • A happiness curve similar to that of humans appears in other animals, hinting that biology may play a part.
  • Seeing a heavy stretch as widely shared, not a personal failing, can support self-compassion and hope.

As you approach 50, you might find that life feels more challenging than it did a few years ago. Maybe it’s the combination of kids, work, and the never-ending daily tasks. Things can feel as though they’re shifting in a more demanding direction. In moments like these, turning to research can offer some reassurance and help you make sense of what you’re experiencing.

Research Finds a U-Shaped Happiness Curve

The economist David Blanchflower analyzed life satisfaction in 145 countries and found the same pattern almost everywhere: higher in youth, lowest in midlife (around age 50), then climbing again, peaking in our 70s (Blanchflower, 2021). On average, it’s a U-shape.

It gets stranger. In a study of 508 chimpanzees and orangutans, people who knew each ape well rated its well-being, and a similar U-shape appeared (Weiss et al., 2012). Isn’t it incredible? Whatever this dip is, it is not only about mortgages and career ambitions. It may be a more universal, shared experience.

Understanding the Midlife Dip Can Offer Context and Hope

Here is what I take from it. A dip is a shape on a graph, not a verdict on your life. If you’re in one, or sitting with someone who is, it may help to know that the road keeps going. It might not change how you feel right now, but it gives you two gifts:

  1. Context: You know you're not alone. Understanding that many people your age around the world share your challenge is important because this “shared humanity”—the experiences many of us have in common—is an essential piece of self-compassion.
  2. Hope: It gives you hope to know that from here, it can be an upward spiral. As we get older, happiness tends to increase.

Why the Happiness Curve May Be Changing

One honest caution: Averages describe groups, not individuals, and the pattern may be shifting. In more recent data, the midlife dip has largely faded, mostly because young people’s mental health has worsened (Blanchflower et al., 2024). So the curve is changing, and that deserves our attention, too. Still, for those of us in midlife, the message holds: The middle can feel heavy, and later life tends to feel better, on average.

Finding Your Place on the Happiness Curve With Self-Compassion

So where does that leave us? Perhaps with a gentler question than “What’s wrong with me?” Try asking, “Where am I on the curve?” Picture the U, and find your spot. Are you sliding down the left side, resting at the bottom, or already starting to climb? Then imagine yourself 10 years further along the right-hand side, looking back at this moment. What would that person want you to know? I suspect they would be kinder to you than you might be towards yourself right now. The dip is a stretch of road, and you are not walking it alone.

Wherever you are on the U-shape, it helps to know the trend. You might be able to beat the dip, but if you can’t, take comfort in knowing you are in good company.

item.title: The New State Laws Defining Abuse Without a Single Bruise
item.description:
Domestic Violence

The New State Laws Defining Abuse Without a Single Bruise

Psychological research is starting to reshape how the law defines harm.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Coercive control describes patterns of psychological abuse that occur without physical violence.
  • Hawaii is the only U.S. state to criminalize coercive control outright; others rely on civil courts.
  • A major meta-analysis links coercive control to PTSD and depression, even without physical harm.
  • Police reports rarely capture coercive control, though it may predict violence better than history.

For decades, the legal system treated intimate partner abuse mainly as a series of discrete physical events: a slap, a shove, a broken bone. Although some laws addressing domestic violence have covered certain forms of nonphysical misconduct, including threats, stalking, and harassment, legal protections have historically focused more heavily on identifiable incidents than on sustained patterns of psychological control. Psychological research describes something different: a sustained pattern of control that can cause serious harm without ever leaving a visible injury. The law is only beginning to catch up.

Coercive control refers to an ongoing pattern of behavior in which one partner isolates, monitors, intimidates, or manipulates the other in order to restrict their independence. It can include controlling access to money, tracking a partner's phone or location, dictating what they wear or eat, or threatening to damage their relationships with family and friends.

Although some of these tactics may independently constitute criminal offenses, such as stalking, harassment, or unlawful threats, others may not be criminal when considered in isolation. Their cumulative effect can therefore be difficult to address under laws focused on individual incidents rather than patterns of conduct.

The Substantial Psychological Evidence of Coercive Control's Harm

Research has found a measurable association between coercive control and adverse mental-health outcomes, including PTSD and depression. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis, titled "The Trauma and Mental Health Impacts of Coercive Control," examined the relationship between coercive control and mental health outcomes including post-traumatic stress disorder, complex PTSD, and depression across the available evidence.

This is important, because some legal frameworks addressing domestic abuse focus on discrete acts of violence, threats, or other prohibited conduct rather than the cumulative psychological effects of a sustained pattern of control. Research associating coercive control with serious psychological harm, even in the absence of physical violence, supports examining whether existing legal protections adequately address the cumulative effects of controlling behavior.

Why Coercive Control Is Hard to Spot

The difficulty isn't limited to courtrooms. Research examining how police officers document intimate partner violence has found that indicators of coercive control appear in fewer than one in ten police reports, with the exception of psychological abuse, which was noted in roughly 28 percent of cases. The low documentation rate may reflect, among other things, the difficulty of identifying a pattern of conduct during an incident-based police response.

That gap has consequences beyond documentation. One analysis found that certain indicators of coercive control were more predictive of subsequent intimate partner violence than prior incidents of violence alone, suggesting that assessments focused exclusively on past physical incidents may overlook important warning signs.

Legislatures Are Starting to Respond

England and Wales criminalized controlling and coercive behavior in 2015. Momentum has been slower but real in the United States. A growing number of states—including California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Vermont, and Washington—have expressly recognized coercive control or coercive controlling behavior in their domestic-violence, civil protection-order, or related family-law frameworks. Most of these provisions operate through civil remedies or family-law proceedings, rather than establishing coercive control as a standalone criminal offense.

Hawaii remains the only state identified in recent nationwide legal analyses as having expressly criminalized coercive control itself, rather than addressing it solely through civil protections or other existing criminal offenses. Under Hawaii law, the conduct is punishable as a petty misdemeanor; in 2026 the state legislature extended that provision through June 2031.

As more jurisdictions recognize coercive control, courts will face questions about how to evaluate patterns of conduct, distinguish abusive behavior from legitimate relationship conflicts, and apply statutory standards consistently. Expert testimony may help explain the psychological effects of coercive control in appropriate cases, although its necessity and admissibility will depend on the governing law and circumstances. Closing the gap between how control is experienced and how it can be proven remains an open question.

item.title: Whose Dream Is It? Why We Pursue Music Lessons
item.description:
Education

Whose Dream Is It? Why We Pursue Music Lessons

Early expectations may shape what you hope to gain from music.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Music lessons are often driven by parental regrets or one's desire for social admiration.
  • Motivation often stems from a psychological shift to move from inferiority to competency.
  • A productive orientation frees musicians from the toxic trap of seeking public approval.

What are our intentions when we sign ourselves or our children up for music lessons? Do we entertain visions of great accomplishment, accompanied by great admiration from others? Do we imagine being noticed, respected, or envied by others whom we feel have not recognized, have ignored, or have dismissed us in the past? Is our desire for our children to learn an instrument entangled with our own regrets and feelings of failure? Do we desire to enjoy learning an instrument, or is something else driving us?

These are important questions to ask oneself when taking music lessons, and are at the heart of the question of process-focused versus product-focused motivation.

How the Ideal Self and Childhood Expectations Shape Motivation

Motivation is a highly individual process, and manifests from the tapestry of our past, our current circumstances, as well as the vision of the future we hold for ourselves. We call this future version of ourselves the ideal self, which we measure our current or actual self against. Our imagined future self is often a solution to feelings of inadequacy or inferiority that come from what we learned in childhood about parental, social, and cultural expectations.

Parents have the additional responsibility of remaining clear about what is our own unfinished business and what is the true interest of our child. Whose dream is it?

These are complicated considerations that, when sorted out and resolved before pursuing music lessons, can set the stage for a healthier, more enjoyable, and more effective learning experience. Two thinkers, Alfred Adler and Erich Fromm, offer useful insights into dealing with issues of this kind.

Adler's Insight

Alfred Adler described the benefits of understanding motivation as a desire to move from a sense of inferiority to a place of superiority. Superiority, in Adlerian terms, can manifest in two ways: as a healthful fulfillment of what one feels they could be, and, in its malignant form, a desire to control or dominate others. Different people are driven by different motivations, but they can all be understood as a shift from a position of deficit to a position of surplus, from a place of I'm not good enough to a place of I'm okay. In its pathological extreme, this motivation is driven to an extreme attitude of I'm better than others. This is what we call narcissism.

Fromm's Solution

Fetishized desire for admiration, being envied, or a preoccupation with being respected are hallmark qualities of malignant narcissism. Erich Fromm described these qualities of the marketing character type, which has become the celebrated norm of the social media generation. This pursuit, Fromm tells us, is empty and will eventually result in moral and spiritual despair. The healthful, mature solution to the natural feelings of inferiority can be described by what Fromm called the productive orientation of character.

Productive orientation is characterized by Fromm as: growth-oriented rather than goal-oriented, productive rather than stagnant, interested in the living biological rather than the dead artificial, and active thought rather than passive acceptance of social conventions. In other words, the productive character focuses on the process rather than the product.

Process vs. Product

Applying this lesson to music study allows us to free ourselves and our children from the unhealthful expectations of judgment, comparison to others, and the misuse of music to settle past scores with those we feel have abused us. The focus on process transforms the learning experience from a means to an end to an end in itself. The daily practice of sitting with the instrument, growing in our abilities from day to day, and enjoying the fruits of our daily commitment to working at the instrument affords a joy in the process of learning that is free from the judgmental expectations that so often contaminate the experience for most of us. We can find joy in simply working and playing music, without the approval, disapproval, acceptance, or rejection from others. This is an attitude of learning an instrument without the expectation of anything other than learning it to the best of our abilities.
